item.title: Quantum-like Architecture of the Social Atom: Mental Marker Coherence and the Triple-Resonance Mechanism of Cognitive Activation
item.description: arXiv:2610.12472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social Laser Theory (SLT) provides a rigorous quantum-like mathematical formalism for modeling collective social activation. While its macroscopic effects mimic laser physics, the fundamental driver of the lasing regime resides in the internal state dynamics of the social atom. In this paper, we propose a quantum-like architecture for the individual cognitive system, formalizing the social atom as a composite quantum system where mental markers - spanning cognitive, affective, and valence dimensions - are represented as internal degrees of freedom in a complex Hilbert space. We show that social activation is not a classical linear response but is governed by a Triple-Resonance Mechanism: the simultaneous quantum-like matching of semantic topic, energetic impact, and valence stance between the agent's internal state and the informational field. We detail how the repeated processing of quantized informational units (infons) leads to a state of cognitive population inversion. We further establish a link to Human Entanglement Theory (HET), suggesting that the emergence of coherent informational fields is rooted in the phase alignment of these internal mental markers across a population. By situating SLT within the broader framework of Social Quantum Field Theory (SQFT), this paper provides a neuro-cognitive foundation for collective phenomena such as emotional contagion and rapid narrative amplification. Our results suggest that the Social Laser is a macroscopic manifestation of quantum-like effects across the human cognitive and neuro-social architecture.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Khrennikov, Christian Aspalter, Likan Zhan

item.title: Insurance perspectives on climate-related risks
item.description: arXiv:2610.12473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emerging climate risks are bringing pressing challenges for insurers globally, as they face growing uncertainty in quantifying climate impacts from physical and transition risks. Climate risks are broad and can manifest through short-term changes and events, as well as long-term and sometimes irreversible changes, such as sea level rise and temperature increases. Significant economic changes are inevitable as countries transition and adapt to mitigate climate-related risks. Given the wide range of potential implications for insurers, we conducted a series of interviews with insurance practitioners and academic researchers to explore the diverse landscape of current perspectives on climate-related risks. The interviews considered how insurers can manage emerging climate risks and the role of pricing as a signal of risk. In the context of unknown unknowns for insurers in understanding long-term impacts of climate change, we identify the importance of scenario analysis in informing forward-looking drivers of change and the importance it plays in meeting evolving regulatory requirements.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Dong, Aaron Bruhn, Francis K. C. Hui, Han Lin Shang

item.title: Voluntary nonpharmaceutical intervention as a feedback-evolving game
item.description: arXiv:2610.12519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as mask wearing, can reduce epidemic spread, but their effectiveness depends on whether people adopt and sustain them. The incentive to adhere changes with infection risk and with the behavior of others. Yet it remains unclear how epidemiological protection and social reinforcement determine the strategic structure of infection control, and how epidemic feedback changes that structure over time. Here, we develop a socio-epidemiological model in which prevalence changes behavioral incentives while adherence changes transmission, separating private protection from source control and incorporating conformity. At a given prevalence, private protection favors adherence, source control creates opportunities for free-riding, and conformity reinforces whichever behavior is already common, generating distinct adherence games. Because adherence reduces transmission and prevalence, the population can move between these games as the epidemic unfolds. This feedback can stabilize partial adherence, create alternative behavioral norms, or generate recurrent epidemic-behavior cycles. Moreover, interventions with the same population-level effect on transmission at a given adherence level can produce different long-term outcomes when protection is distributed differently between the individual and others. Thus, voluntary infection control is a feedback-evolving game whose outcome depends not only on epidemiological efficacy but also on who is protected and how behavior is socially reinforced.
item.dc:creator: Ryuichi Kumata, Hiromu Ito, Masato Yamamichi

item.title: Learning Social Influence with Unobserved Attention
item.description: arXiv:2610.12616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social influence, the tendency of our social environment to sway our beliefs and behaviors, is often cited as a driver of population-level trends in opinions or beliefs. Many quantitative theories of social influence assume that an agent interacts with its entire social environment. This assumption is often unrealistic. For example, users of online platforms typically see posts from only a small subset of the accounts they follow at any given time. We introduce a simple probabilistic agent-based model of social influence that explicitly models unobserved attention mechanisms. The first of these latent mechanisms is selection: each agent interacts with only one other agent at a time from its social environment. The second is retention: the agent chooses whether or not to ignore the opinion of the other. Our model admits an efficient maximum-likelihood algorithm which allows us to fit it to opinion traces even when these mechanisms are unobserved. On synthetic data, omitting either latent mechanism reduces the overall strength of social influence governed by the inferred interaction kernel, which hides the evidence for the underlying nonlinearity of the social influence. We study a selection of previously analyzed empirical datasets and curate several new ones. We show that models that include the latent mechanisms are often more predictive on these datasets; indeed, they typically improve prediction far more than the choice of interaction kernel does. Modeling latent attention increases held-out predictive likelihood on 14 of these 15 datasets. Each mechanism changes the size of the inferred kernel in a predictable direction, while its effect on the kernel's shape depends on the data.
item.dc:creator: William Thompson, Moyi Tian, Linh Huynh, Alexander Wiedemann, Vicki Modisette, Philip S. Chodrow, Heather Z. Brooks

item.title: A data-driven heuristic-ensemble method for behavioural inference in collective-risk dilemma experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.13595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The collective-risk dilemma has become a paradigm for studying cooperation in a wide variety of social experiments, initiatives that generate increasingly rich datasets describing individual actions over successive decision-making processes. Beyond the purely descriptive analysis of such empirical datasets, a methodological framework is required to interpret and reproduce the observed dynamics, a scheme that may be skewed by exogenous biases. Here, we introduce a data-driven, non-parametric method for simulating individual decisions together with a validation protocol for assessing the fidelity level of the outcomes they generate. Our methodological contribution is based on an empirical heuristic ensemble: agents are represented by a finite set of behavioural heuristics, probabilities conditioned on different observable features of the game state, endowed with a hard-voting arbitration that determines their per-round final decisions. This reproducible generative framework allows for behavioural inference in different collective-risk dilemma setups: Behavioural heuristics are seeded directly from empirical data assessing conditional probabilities, without a priori assumptions; a plurality vote with uniform random tie-breaking resolves between competing heuristics each round, adding no free parameters; validation follows a pattern-oriented approach, comparing synthetic and empirical macro-indicators against single-heuristic and uniform-random baselines; synthetic data generated allow exploration of scenarios or experimental setups that have not been empirically realised; as a worked example, we instantiate our methodological approach on the xAire citizen science collective-risk dilemma experiment run in Barcelona.
item.dc:creator: Marc Sadurn\'i, Mart\'in F. D\'iaz, Josep Perell\'o, Miquel Montero

item.title: Modelling the complex dynamics of online disinformation cascades
item.description: arXiv:2610.13839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disinformation on online social media has been on the rise in the past years. While there is extensive literature modelling social cascades, online disinformation cascades show distinctive characteristics: they provoke debunking reactions, they spread over networks with heterogeneous connectivity, and they compete for the limited attention of users --- which recommendation algorithms may partly offset. We propose a model including these ingredients and study it through Monte--Carlo simulations and mean--field approximations, on random graphs and an empirical Twitter network. We find that debunking reactions are double--edged: they reduce the reach of appealing items but allow unappealing ones to reach audiences they would not otherwise reach. Degree heterogeneity makes cascades trigger at a much lower content appeal but limits their final reach: heterogeneous networks are easy to ignite yet hard to saturate. Limited attention cancels the effects from degree heterogeneity, although the mediation of recommendation algorithms may restore them.
item.dc:creator: Guillermo Romero Moreno, Valentin Robu, Han La Poutr\'{e}

item.title: Separating Field--Camp Alignment from Structural Balance in a Frustrated Random-Field Ising Model of Social Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.12578v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frustrated Ising models of social networks mix ferromagnetic (agreement-seeking) and antiferromagnetic (antagonistic) couplings, and the antagonistic bonds are almost always placed independently at a fixed rate, yielding a +/-J spin glass. Real signed networks (Epinions, Slashdot, Wikipedia) instead show an excess of balanced triads, and perfectly balanced placement is gauge-equivalent to an unfrustrated ferromagnet. We compare three sign-placement conditions on a frustrated random-field Ising model of a polarised population, sharing an identical graph, field assignment, and edge-weight magnitudes: an independent baseline; a balance-structured condition whose camp membership coincides with each voter's field sign; and the same condition with camp labels randomly permuted, so triadic balance is identical by construction while the camp-field correlation is removed. On a confound-controlled Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the sampled energy-gap distribution (simulated annealing), the aligned condition differs from the baseline at every density tested (p = 7.3e-8), while the permuted condition shows no significant difference (paired mean difference 0.003, 95% CI [-0.041, 0.046]). Field-camp alignment, not triadic balance alone, drives the effect. The qualitative direction follows from a known mapping; the contribution is a quantitative, confound-controlled measurement of the effect's size away from that limit, robust to parallel-tempering sampling, system sizes up to N = 300, and structural noise calibrated to real networks, while triadic balance alone produces no detectable effect at N = 90 and at most a small one at N = 180-300 (paired change in KS distance about 0.04, 95% CI upper bound below 0.09).
item.dc:creator: Natalia Romero

item.title: Credit Attribution in Timestamped Soccer Networks Using Multivariate Hawkes Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.12775v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The two main traditional player statistics used in soccer are goals scored and assists, with an assist credited when a player's pass immediately leads to a teammate scoring. Attributing credit solely to the player who makes the final pass before a goal fails to account for the contributions of multiple players in the buildup to the goal. Consequently, traditional statistics provide only a limited view of player involvement. In this paper, we use multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs) to model timestamped sequences of passes and shots, which form continuous-time networks. MHPs provide a branching mechanism where an event (a pass or shot) can be generated as a child of a previous event, which allows us to quantify each pass's contribution to a subsequent pass or shot. This approach distributes credit across multiple passes within an attacking sequence, making it applicable across a wide range of situations. Building on this framework, we propose expected goal involvements (xGI), a metric that measures a player's involvement in creating goal scoring opportunities based on their passes. This metric identifies players who play key roles in creating goal scoring opportunities even if they do not make the final pass, offering a more comprehensive measure of attacking involvement and player performance.
item.dc:creator: Phillip W. Kornberg, Kevin S. Xu

item.title: A Review on the Properties and Nature of Light
item.description: arXiv:2610.13932v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The following paper is a detailed review on the properties and nature in relation to the phenomena known as 'light'. The paper tries to chronologically detail the development of theories and related experiments from the philosophical Greco-Roman and Indian schools of thought to the modern quantum theories.
item.dc:creator: Prachurjo Dutta Roy

item.title: Coupling with opinion dynamics promotes prosocial behavior in multilayer networks
item.description: arXiv:2601.00460v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Various theoretical and empirical studies have accounted for why humans cooperate in competitive environments. Although prior work has revealed that network structure and multiplex interactions can promote cooperation, most theory assumes that individuals play dilemma games in all social contexts. However, real-world agents may participate in a diversity of interactions, not all of which present dilemmas. We develop an evolutionary game model on multilayer networks in which one layer supports the prisoner's dilemma game, while the other follows constant-selection dynamics, representing biased but non-dilemmatic competition, akin to opinion or fad spreading. Our theoretical analysis reveals that coupling a social dilemma layer to a non-dilemmatic constant-selection layer robustly enhances cooperation in many cases, across different multilayer networks, updating rules, and payoff schemes. These findings suggest that embedding individuals within diverse networked settings---even those unrelated to direct social dilemmas---can be a principled approach to engineering cooperation in socio-ecological and organizational systems.
item.dc:creator: Jnanajyoti Bhaumik, Naoki Masuda

item.title: Systemic risk in interbank networks: disentangling balance sheets and network effects
item.description: arXiv:2109.14360v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how the level of systemic risk empirically observed in an interbank network differs from the expected risk implied by the balance sheets composition of the participating banks, abstracting from the specific configuration of bilateral exposures. To this end, using different contagion models (i.e., interbank asset valuation functions), we measure observed systemic risk on e-MID network data from 2005 to 2012 and compare it with the expected risk generated by a null model: an ensemble of interbank networks whose links represent possible market clearing configurations. This counterfactual is obtained through a maximum-entropy approach that preserves banks' balance sheet variables and diversification patterns, while randomizing the configuration of exposures. We find that the aggregate levels of observed and expected systemic risks are generally consistent but diverge significantly during turbulent periods - specifically following the default of Lehman Brothers (2009) and the VLTRO implementation by the ECB (2012). At the individual level, however, banks often appear more or less risky than implied by their balance sheet alone, due to their position in the network. Our results show, on the one hand, that balance sheet information embedded in a suitable maximum-entropy framework provides reliable estimates of aggregate systemic risk; on the other hand, they highlight the importance of detailed network information for accurate stress testing of individual banks, particularly after systemic events.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Ferracci, Giulio Cimini
